title: Amauropelma grasshoffi Jäger, 2026, sp. nov.
abstract: Amauropelma grasshoffi sp. nov. Figs 1–2, 43–44, 89 Type material. THE PHILIPPINES: Calabarzon Region: Holotype male, Laguna Province, Los Baños, Mt Makiling [14° 8'54.86"N, 121°14'1.45"E, 157 m], jungle litter, P.T. Lehtinen leg. 16 November 1979 (SMF). Additional material examined. 3 subadult males, 4 juveniles, with same data as for holotype (SMF). Etymology. The species honours Dr. Manfred Grasshoff on occasion of his 90 th birthday, for serving as arachnology curator in the Senckenberg Research Institute for so many years and for his outstanding contributions on Araneidae, especially functional aspects of the copulatory organs; name in genitive case. Diagnosis. Small Ctenidae (total length male 4.9).Males of Amauropelma grasshoffi sp. nov. can be distinguished from those of all other congeners by the following combination of characters (Figs 1–2): 1. Tegulum with a retrodistal knob, 2. TA large, arising subcentrally, with roundish retrolateral and pointed prolateral part, 3. RTA with elongated base and 2 apices, 4. RPA present, but indistinct. Description. Male (holotype). PL 2.7, PW 2.1, AW 1.1, OL 2.2, OW 1.4. Eye diameters and interdistances: AME 0.13, ALE 0.13, PME 0.17, PLE 0.18, AME–AME 0.08, AME–ALE 0.14, PME–PME 0.07, PME–PLE 0.20, AME–PME 0.04, ALE–PLE 0.10, clypeus AME 0.08, clypeus ALE 0.20. Palp and leg measurements: palp 3.15 (0.9, 0.55, 0.5, –, 1.2), I 8.2 (2.2, 1.1, 2.1, 1.7, 1.1), II 6.95 (2.0, 0.95, 1.7, 1.4, 0.9), III 6.7 (1.9, 0.9, 1.5, 1.5, 0.9), IV 9.3 (2.5, 1.0, 2.2, 2.4, 1.2). Leg formula 4123. Spination of palp and legs: palp 13(0)0, 100, 1011; femora I p002, d111, r011, II–III p012, d111, r012, IV p012, d111, r001; patellae I–II 000, III–IV 101; tibiae I–II p010, v22222, III–IV p11, d111, r11, v222; metatarsi I v222, II p010, r010, v222, III p112, d010, r112, v222, IV p112, d010, r112, v322. Chelicerae with 3 promarginal, 4+2(1) retromarginal teeth. Margin of chelicerae close to fang base with 1 escort seta. Palp as in diagnosis (Figs 1–2). Cymbium tip roughly triangular with rounded tip. RTA arising retrolaterally from sub-distal tibia, both tips retrolaterad in ventral view, disto-dorsad in retrolateral view. Embolus arising at 8.30-o’clock-position, conductor at 1.30-o’clock-position, TA subcentrally at 7.30-o’clock-position from tegulum. Embolus large, semicircular, distally with transparent flange, tip pointed, proximo-retrolaterad. Colouration (Figs 43–44). Deep yellowish-brown to brown. Dorsum of prosoma with fovea marked and faint lateral bands and marginal stripes. Sternum, venter of coxae, labium and gnathocoxae light yellowish-brown. Chelicerae deep yellowish-brown with dark grey pattern. Legs yellowish-brown, distal segments darker. OS yellowish-brown, dorsally with irregular pattern; ventrally with dots in posterior half. Female. Unknown. Distribution. Known only from the type locality (Fig. 89). First record of Amauropelma for the Philippines.

title: Bowie soundandvision Jäger, 2026, sp. nov.
abstract: Bowie soundandvision sp. nov. Figs 105–110, 115–122, 146 Type material. THAILAND: Nan Province: Holotype male, Doi Phu Ka, 19°12'0.44"N, 101°4'53.51"E, 1200 m, hill evergreen forest, habitat A, O. Kosulic leg. 28 May 2024 (SMF). Paratypes. 1 male, 1 female, with same data as for holotype (1 male: CUNHM; 1 female: SMF). Additional material examined. THAILAND: Nan Province: 1 subadult male, with same data as for holotype (SMF). Etymology. This species is named after the song “Sound and vision” by David Bowie; name in apposition. Diagnosis. Small to medium-sized Ctenidae (total length male 9.0–10.3, female 10.5). Distinguished from other males of the bemywife group by (Figs 116–118) 1. Cymbial extension on retromargin long and pointed, 2. TA with obtuse angle enclosed by the two parts (cymbial extension shorter and blunt in B. bemywife, B. kosulici sp. nov. and B. yulin, and TA with right angle enclosed by two parts in B. kosulici sp. nov.; see Figs 91–93, Jäger 2022: figs 314–316). Females distinguished from those of the bemywife group by (Figs 120–122) 1. Spermathecal chambers continuous in ventral view, 2. Median plate ventrally concave in posterior view (separated in B. kosulici sp. nov. and B. weepingwall sp. nov., median plate ventrally flat in posterior view in B. bemywife; see Figs 94–96, Jäger 2022: figs 317–319). Description. Male (holotype). PL 4.8, PW 3.8, AW 1.9, OL 4.2, OW 2.6. Eye diameters and interdistances: AME 0.23, ALE 0.18, PME 0.34, PLE 0.33, AME–AME 0.15, AME–ALE 0.30, PME–PME 0.15, PME–PLE 0.30, AME–PME 0.07, ALE–PLE 0.14, clypeus AME 0.13, clypeus ALE 0.39. Palp and leg measurements: palp 5.9 (2.2, 0.9, 1.0, - 1.8), I 14.8 (3.8, 1.7, 4.1, 3.9, 1.3), II missing, III 12.2 (3.7, 1.5, 2.8, 3.1, 1.1), IV 15.3 (4.3, 1.6, 3.9, 5.0, 1.5). Leg formula 413. Spination of palp and legs (II missing): palp 141, 000, 1010; femora I p021, d111, r1(2)11, III p112, d111, r112, IV p112, d111, r002; patellae I 001, III–IV 101; tibiae I p10, d111, r11, v22222, III–IV p11, d111, r11, v222; metatarsi I p111, r111, v222, III p112, d010, r112, v222, IV p112, d010, r112, v21112. Chelicerae with 3 promarginal, 4 retromarginal teeth, and with ca. 13 denticles in a single row along the entire furrow. Margin of chelicerae close to fang base with 1 strong and 3 thinner escort setae. Coxae ventrally densely covered with short, strong setae, density increasing from I to IV. Fe to Ti I–IV without apically curved setae, but with sparse cover of short setae (Fig. 110). Palp as in diagnosis (Figs 116–118). RTA arising in distal half from tibia. Retro-proximal cymbial bulge with convex margin. Embolus arising at 7.30- to 8-o’clock-position, conductor at 12.30-o’clock-position, tegular apophysis at 6-o’clock-position from tegulum. Embolus with opening of spermophor dorsally, subapically with tiny slit seen in distal view. Tegulum with membranous, conductor-like structure, ending close to embolus. Tegular apophysis with rough surface, extending retrolaterally very slightly beyond tegular margin. Colouration (Figs 105–106). Yellowish-brown. Median band on prosoma distinctly delimited by dark lines continuing laterally as marbled pattern. Sternum, venter of coxae, labium and gnathocoxae yellowish-brown without pattern, sternum slightly darker. Chelicerae reddish-brown. Legs yellowish-brown with distal segments darker. Dorsal opisthosoma with bright heart region, anteriorly delimited by pair of dark patches, posteriorly only less distinctly delimited with 3 pairs of dark patches. Ventral opisthosoma with median field filled with dark patches and longitudinal lines of light indistinct patches. Spinnerets and anal tubercle bright, surroundings dark. Female (paratype). PL 4.2, PW 3.6, AW 2.4, OL 5.8, OW 4.2. Eye diameters and interdistances: AME 0.24, ALE 0.20, PME 0.35, PLE 0.31, AME–AME 0.15, AME–ALE 0.34, PME–PME 0.16, PME–PLE 0.35, AME–PME 0.10, ALE–PLE 0.18, clypeus AME 0.13, clypeus ALE 0.40. Palp and leg measurements: palp 5.1 (1.7, 0.9, 1.1, –, 1.4), I 11.8 (3.3, 1.8, 3.0, 2.6, 1.1), II 11.2 (3.1, 1.6, 2.9, 2.5, 1.1), III 10.3 (3.1, 1.4, 2.4, 2.4, 1.0), IV 14.7 (4.0, 1.5, 3.5, 4.3, 1.4). Leg formula 4123. Spination of palp and legs: palp 131, 100, 1211, 1013; femora I p021, d111, r110, II p112, d111, r1(2)10, III p112, d111, r111, IV p112, d111, r001; patellae I–II 000, III–IV 101; tibiae I–II v22222, III–IV p11, d111, r11, v222; metatarsi I–II v222, III p112, d010, r112, v222, IV p112, d010, r112, v21122. Chelicerae with 3 promarginal, 4 retromarginal teeth, and with ca. 10 denticles in a row along the entire furrow. Margin of chelicerae close to fang base with 1 strong and 4 thinner escort setae. Fe to Ti I–IV with apically curved setae (Fig. 109). Copulatory organ as in diagnosis (Figs 120–122). Epigyne wider than long, with 3 pairs of slit sensilla, anterior bands integrated in field. Median plate with bulging lateral margins. Bases of lateral teeth extending beyond median plate margin in posterior view. Spermathecae close to each other, separated by less than chamber I diameter. Colouration (Figs 107–108). As in male, but opisthosoma generally fainter. Variation. Male: PL 5.8, OL 4.5. Slightly darker than holotype and RTA with tiny tooth subapically. Distribution. Known only from the type locality in the Nan Province in northern Thailand (Figs 115, 146).

title: Ecological insights into spider diversity and behaviour in Chhattisgarh: A review
venue: International Journal of Advanced Biochemistry Research
abstract: Spiders, belonging to the order Araneae, represent one of the most diverse and ecologically significant groups of arthropods, playing critical roles in maintaining ecological balance as both predators and prey. Despite their ecological importance, regional studies on spider diversity and behavior remain limited in several parts of India, including the state of Chhattisgarh. This review consolidates current knowledge on the diversity, taxonomy, behavior, and ecological functions of spiders documented in Chhattisgarh across various habitats, including forests, grasslands, agricultural fields, and urban ecosystems. The review highlights the rich taxonomic diversity of spiders in the region, comprising over 220 species across 96 genera and 23 families, with prominent families such as Araneidae, Thomisidae, Salticidae, and Gnaphosidae being well represented (Choudhury et al. 2024; Nichat et al. 2025). Behavioral observations indicate a wide range of adaptations in web-building, foraging, mating, and diurnal/nocturnal activity patterns. Field surveys conducted using techniques such as sweep netting, pitfall trapping, visual inspection, and web mapping have revealed significant seasonal and habitat-based variations in spider community composition, strongly influenced by monsoon cycles and habitat structure (Kujur & Ekka, 2016; Gajbe, 2007). Additionally, the review discusses the vital role of spiders in natural pest regulation, contributing to ecosystem stability and offering potential applications in sustainable agriculture. Threats such as habitat destruction, pesticide exposure, and climate change are also examined, along with the urgent need for spider conservation initiatives and public awareness. Future research priorities include taxonomic revisions, molecular systematics, long-term ecological monitoring, and the exploration of spiders’ potential in biotechnology and pest management. By synthesizing available scientific literature and recent field reports, this review serves as a foundational resource for researchers, conservationists, and policymakers aiming to promote arachnid biodiversity research and conservation in Chhattisgarh.

title: The Midnight Shift
abstract: He hurts her with his eyes shut and his tongue poked out and the smell of hamburgers still on his fingers. Two Big Boy Special Burgers with the Lot, double cheese and sauce but no beetroot. I know exactly, because it's either me or Vorna who gets them ready. Sometimes when ordering, he'll say that just for something different I can make it hot dogs with yellow mustard. It is nothing new for him to have two cartons of chips along with a chocolate malted thickshake. No wonder he is such a shape. Like a Huntsman spider with a swollen belly. And all day clinging over a power drive steering wheel with the vinyl seating getting hot in the afternoon sun.She tries not to touch the moles that are spongy on his shoulders. Some have hairs growing out the middle. She watches them while he grunts, and the sweat that beads along his skin. Once a piece of earwax fell out. It rolled down her face like a tear.His neck is bull red and I think that if she only dared to bite that throbbing vein he would die. The blood would spurt high in the air and pattern her skies more brilliant than any sunset.Standing behind the front counter I can see the sunsets. Between busloads of hamburger eaters I watch them spatter, streak, light up, glow yellow, look like jam or flower colours, go smokey, go gold, go mauve, Go Shell. Go Well With Shell. Across the highway, the other service station interrupts my view. It is a decrepit building that sprawls in dim oblong shapes by the side of the road, but the Shell sign is always lighted by dusk. Five minutes before it, Mulvy Smith who runs this place switches on our Golden Fleece ram. For a while after I started work at the Roadhouse, I tried to think of original ways to see the sun through the falling clouds. The same way I used to learn a new word from the dictionary every day. Like my attempts to improve my vocabulary, all efforts have faded. My mind overloads with other people's sunset descriptions and the smell of chips in their boiling vats.By sundown, Vorna, who arranges the salads for the sit-down people, is telling me about her aunt who has been in the nursing home for donkey's years.`Those chips ready to go love?' she asks, making the rolls of Kraftsliced stand straight in rings of tinned pineapple. `It's a crying shame.' She is slicing the buttered bread into triangles. The crusts are only a bit stale. `For all those years she's just a little Bean. A vegetable, you know. And now after all this they decide to operate. Diverticulitis it was. Got to wear a bag now. A colostomy.' Vorna finds the word she is looking for and spills grease from a chiko roll down her yellow zippered uniform. It coagulates in the metal teeth as the rest of the night passes.Above the floor that gets slimy with fallen foods, above the two garbage bins filling with multi-colouring pig slops, higher than the washing up sinks and the clock, is a strip of glass. Suns only set in the west when I'm out the front and serving at the counter. In the kitchen all I can see are the trains going past. First comes the cold chrome clanking as they slow down at the edge of the town lights. Through the high thin window I see the wooden overpass bridge bending and shaking. It seems that the bridge is right above the kitchen. I imagine disasters. Falling passengers scattering the trays of buns I butter. People splashing into the egg and milk mix the floured cutlets have to be dunked into. Sleeping babies in bunny rugs screaming awake as they crash-land in the chocolate sauce bucket.The air is lonelier after the train noises die. The night shift is the sad shift. The sound of the swings outside in the empty picnic area gives me the shivers. Vorna drops Winfield 25 ash into burgers and the other counter girl goes home. My banana thickshake dinner tastes of chemicals. I eat cold chips one by one to disguise the taste. Vorna drops a whole butt on top of a steak and egg sandwich and covers it in a pool of barbeque sauce. …

title: Preface
Ctenus monaghani Jäger, 2013, spec. nov.
abstract: Ctenus monaghani spec. nov. Figs 1 –9 Type material. Holotype male (SMF), Laos, Khammouan Province, E Thakek, Ban Kouanphavang, N 17°27.150', E 104°56.321', 180 m altitude, secondary forest close to limestone cliff, leaf litter, by hand, at night, P. Jäger leg. 29.IV.2012. Etymology. This species is named in honour of the British actor Dominic Monaghan who filmed together with the author in Laos for the documentary show “Wild Things”; Dom’s enthusiasm for nature in general, and spiders and other little respected animals in particular, was the driving force behind the production of this documentary; name in genitive. Diagnosis. Medium-sized Ctenidae (total length male 10.0). Similar to C. pulchriventris (Simon, 1897) from Central to South Africa (Benoit 1979) and C. elgonensis Benoit, 1978 from Kenya in lacking a retroproximal cymbial extension and in having the distal margin of RTA transversal to the length axis of the tibia, but clearly distinguished by the oval tegular apophysis from these species. Distinguished from the Asian species C. yaeyamensis Yoshida, 1998 (Japan, Taiwan), C. robustus Thorell, 1897 (Burma, Laos), C. theodorianum Jäger, 2012 (Laos), C. holthoffi Jäger, 2012 (Laos), C. bayeri Jäger, 2012 (Laos) and C. saci Ono, 2010 (Vietnam) by the lack of a retroproximal cymbial extension, and from C. martensi Jäger, 2012 (Nepal), C. ramosus Thorell, 1887 (Burma), C. cladarus Jäger, 2012 (Burma) and C. simplex Thorell, 1897 (Burma, Laos) by the different shape of the RTA. Legs lacking any modifications known from e.g. C. theodorianum (humps on femur, tibia and metatarsus III) or C. simplex (humps on coxae IV), but ventral coxae exhibiting short stout spines (Figs 8–9) similar as in C. holthoffi or C. palembangensis Strand, 1906. Description. Male (holotype). Prosoma length 5.2, prosoma width 3.9, anterior width of prosoma 2.0, opisthosoma length 4.8, opisthosoma width 2.5. Eye diameters and interdistances: AME 0.28, ALE 0.24, PME 0.36, PLE 0.33, AME–AME 0.10, AME–ALE 0.26, PME–PME 0.11, PME–PLE 0.25, AME–PME 0.05, ALE–PLE 0.09, clypeus AME 0.11, clypeus ALE 0.43. Palp and leg measurements: palp 6.2 (2.4, 1.0, 1.2, -, 1.6), I 15.6 (4.1, 2.0, 4.3, 3.8, 1.4), II 12.8 (3.7, 1.9, 3.5, 3.4, 1.3), III 12.2 (3.3, 1.5, 2.8, 3.4, 1.2), IV 17.4 (4.5, 1.8, 4.3, 5.2, 1.6). Leg formula IV-I-II-III. Spination of palp and legs: palp 141, 100, 1010; femora I p003, d111, r112, II p112, d111, r 112, III p112, d111, r112, IV p112, d111, r002; patellae I 100, II–IV 101; tibiae I p010, d100, r110, v22222, II p010, d111, r110, v22222, III–IV p11, d111, r11, v222; metatarsi I–II p111, r111, v222, III p112, r112, v222, IV p112, d010, r112, v21112. Chelicerae with 3 promarginal, 4/5 retromarginal teeth, and with elongated patch of several tiny denticles along entire cheliceral furrow. Retromargin of chelicerae close to fang base with 6 bristles (1 distinctly stronger). Position of tarsal organ: I 0.85, II 0.84, III 0.79, IV 0.71. Palp as in diagnosis (Figs 1–4). RTA arising distally in a right angle from tibia, conical, tip with well defined ridge. Cymbium tip short, slightly conical, retroproximally widened and with small pocket. Embolus arising at 7.30 o’clockposition from tegulum, semicircular in ventral view, short with broad base, conical distally with blunt tip, membranous extension covering proximal half of embolus; circular opening of spermophore situated dorsally. Conductor arising at 12 o’clock-position subdistally. Tegular apophysis arising at 6 o’clock-position from tegulum subcentrally, distinctly excavated on dorsal side. Spermophore visible in retrolateral half, running submarginally along tegular margin. Colour (Figs 5–9). Brown to olive with indistinct pattern. Dorsal prosoma with light median band consisting of white dense hairs, laterally with radial marble-like pattern. Sternum and ventral coxae yellowish-brown without pattern; labium and gnathocoxae darker. Chelicerae as dorsal prosoma with three light stripes in proximal half and with dark distal half. Legs and palp without pattern with hind legs darker. Dorsal opisthosoma with light median band and pairs of dark spots in posterior half. Ventral opisthosoma dark with four posteriorly converging rows of white patches consisting of white hairs. Anterior lateral spinnerets dark, posterior lateral and median spinnerets and anal tubercle light. Female. Unknown. Distribution. Known only from the type locality.

title: Maria Sibylla Merian and Bobbi Wilson: Challenging Inequality Through A Love of Entomology
abstract: An enchanting blend of plants and insects in Maria Sibylla Merian’s botanical illustration, circa 1720. Amidst the vast realms of the natural world, a microcosmos teeming with arthropod secrets exists—a world of vibrant colors, intricate patterns, and extraordinary adaptations. When the insect kingdom beckoned, one remarkable woman, Maria Sybilla Merian (1647–1717), dared to venture into their hidden universe and study their lifestyles and interactions with other living creatures. From cultivating silkworms as a young teenager to studying insect morphology and metamorphosis in Suriname, Merian was a force of nature whose seminal works helped to systemically deconstruct scientific dogma and found the discipline of entomology. (Left): Maria Sibylla Merian (Right): Bobbi Wilson (Photo by Andrew Hurley, Yale University Born on 2 April 1647 in Frankfurt, Germany, Merian was just three years of age when her father, Matthäus Merian, a renowned engraver, died (Rogers 2023). Despite Matthäus’s death early in Maria’s life, the Merian family’s artistic legacy would live on. Merian’s extraordinary drawing ability as a young child was noted by her stepfather, Jacob Marrel, an eminent German painter, who nurtured her abilities and provided her with teachers in his atelier throughout her childhood (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Maria Sibylla Merian made foundational scientific discoveries, developed robust methods for entomology through conducting field research, and pursued ecological endeavors of great scientific importance for entomology. Her work was initially often overlooked as merely a piece of early natural philosophy. However, beginning in the 1970s and subsequent studies of scholarship in the 1980s and 1990s, a re-examination of her work, its originality, and her innovative approach and findings helped establish her pivotal role in laying the foundation for the modern field of entomology, and consequently inspired people of all ages to explore the natural world (Valiant 1992, 1993; Heard 2020). Merian’s descriptions of metamorphosis and her refutation of scientific concepts that had been long entrenched in society played a significant role in bolstering her scientific reputation. Making discoveries and disproving widely accepted scientific beliefs was not always positively received. During Merian’s lifetime, people generally accepted Aristotle’s theory of spontaneous generation, which held that living things could spring from nonliving matter. Scientists and laypeople did not realize that all insects produce eggs and thought that some insects just “spontaneously” grew out of garbage and detritus (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Through Merian’s intensive observation, illustration, and ultimate discovery, she “saw each stage in a bug’s life cycle as a continuous process, when few other naturalists were making connections” between the caterpillar and the butterfly (Swaby 2018; Fig. 1). Merian’s fundamental scientific research on metamorphosis was a nail in the coffin of the antiquated belief in spontaneous generation. Metamorphosis of the Silkworm, Maria Sibylla Merian, 1679. (Wikimedia Commons.) CONSTANTLY SURROUNDED BY PLANTS, INSECTS, AND OTHER ANIMALS, IN ADDITION TO RECEIVING EXPLANATIONS AND WISDOM FROM THE INDIGENOUS PEOPLE, MERIAN WITNESSED THE INTERCONNECTEDNESS OF ECOSYSTEMS WITH A NEW PERSPECTIVE As a result, Merian’s lifetime of field research and artistic study paved the way for the creation of essential scientific methods. At thirteen years old, Merian did not have the resources to fuel her curious mind. No books correctly explained the transitional processes she was observing in insects. She had to conduct her own research, grow her own insects, and generate her own unique hypotheses about insect development (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). To conduct studies, Merian “situated her specimens in context, capturing them crawling on leaves with curing seams, flying over flowers’ stretching tendrils, or circling around stems,” (Swaby 2018). Merian’s distinct approach to scientific observation through an artistic lens set her apart from other illustrators of the time, who solely worked from display cases. She took scrupulous notes and recorded her observations with detailed written descriptions, drawings, and paintings, all of which solidified her live observational methodologies (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018, Beck 2007). Enabled by her home caterpillar farm, Merian drew “pictures in her study book that reflected not only what animals and plants looked like but how they developed” (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Merian’s observations were limited by her own eyes and occasionally looking through a magnifying glass, as microscopy was just beginning to emerge as its own field. With this minimal available technology, the connections Merian made among plants, insects, and animals highlight how much can be learned from careful observations and meticulous record-keeping, further raising the bar for today’s entomologists, who have much more sophisticated tools at their disposal. Merian’s search for opportunities to expand her understanding of the insect world led her to pursue research abroad that set her apart from other naturalists. Merian was “astounded to see what lovely creatures were brought back from the East and West Indies” (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). These species of animals native to South America sparked her interest, so, in June of 1699, Merian, along with her daughter Dorothea, set sail from Amsterdam to Suriname (Rogers 2023). First colonized by the Dutch, Suriname was exploited for its land, and the Indigenous people were forced to work as slaves on plantations that grew sugar, coffee, cocoa, and cotton (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). While many of the colonizers came in search of wealth, Merian was interested in the knowledge that would follow from the exploration of the land’s species. Noting this difference, Merian wrote, “The [Dutch] people there have no desire to investigate such things; indeed they mocked me for seeking something other than sugar in that country” (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). She did not let this cruelty discourage her. With the help of many Indigenous women, Merian and her daughter settled into a home with a quaint garden in the colonies’ capital, Paramaribo, to take on their scientific investigations (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Due to the warm, wet climate, home visits from a diverse collection of vibrant species were common. “Blue lizards laid eggs in the corners of rooms,” “cockroaches that ventured inside were captured for study,” and the garden often welcomed hummingbirds (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Constantly surrounded by plants, insects, and other animals, in addition to receiving explanations and wisdom from the Indigenous people, Merian witnessed the interconnectedness of ecosystems with a new perspective (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). From her two years of consistent observation, Merian was able to publish a collection of watercolor illustrations. As shown in her painting Guava Tree with Huntsman Spider within the collection entitled Insects of Suriname, Merian vividly captured insects, their prey, and the plants in their native tropical environment (Fig. 2). No other scientific artists at the time were publishing work featuring the importance of the interconnectedness between insects and their ecosystems and elucidating predator–prey relationships (Merian 1726). The uniqueness and merit of Merian’s painted illustrations and their corresponding insightful explanations helped her gain access to the male-dominated scientific community. Guava Tree with Huntsman Spider, Orb Weaver Spider, Leaf-Cutter Ants, Army Ants, Cockroach, Tarantulas, and Hummingbird (watercolor). Maria Sibylla Merian, The Insects of Suriname, 1726. Despite the setbacks Merian faced along her scientific and artistic journeys as an orphan, a woman in 17th-century society, and a divorcee, her family’s socioeconomic positioning and national origin meant that she had access to resources that one must consider in the discussion of her success. Although Merian overcame many barriers throughout her artistic and scientific career, her privilege should not go unnoticed. Scientific exploration has been built on the backs of enslaved people, colonization, and Eurocentric ideals. Merian’s access even at a young age to an art studio set her ahead of others interested in discovery. Due to her stepfather’s profession, Merian had an advantage in both her access to artistic education and lessons on scientific observation and note-taking. Women during the 17th century were not allowed to attend art school or universities to formally study science, but Merian had the opportunity to study with her stepfather’s apprentices. She continued to benefit from her family’s wealth into her later life. While Merian “did not approve of the treatment” of the enslaved people, her research in Suriname relied on the traditional knowledge held by Native women regarding the species of insects and plants of the surrounding forests. With the aid of enslaved people, Merian was able to venture into the forest and steer clear of poisonous plants and dangerous animals (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Merian’s life was spent observing insects and their connections to the environment through art. Unlike many other women at the time, she published her findings in many series of collections such as The Caterpillar Book, volumes one, two, and three (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). In these publications, readers can observe how Merian refined her understanding of insect development and unraveled the interdependencies of living creatures across the tree of life. Beyond her scientific achievements, Merian was cognizant of her great privilege and actively worked to end oppressive systems in the Americas by hiring enslaved people, showing her willingness to confront the small-scale challenges of the emerging field of entomology as well as the large-scale problems facing society (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Merian entered the scientific world as a young German girl trying to explore the natural world through an artistic lens. However, she transformed the scientific community with her curiosity for the insect world, and her legacy lives on through the fresh young minds exploring the possibilities of scientific discovery at their fingertips. A modern-day Merian named Bobbi Wilson has recently emerged from her own chrysalis. Wilson’s intrepid curiosity about spotted lanternflies and the insect world has helped her gracefully transcend the barriers of race and gender that sought to extinguish her emerging interests in entomology at the young age of nine (Poitras 2023). While Merian’s full life came to an end centuries ago, her legacy lives on, and Bobbi Wilson’s life in science is just beginning to unfold. Top: Bobbi Wilson labelling lanternflies. Bottom: Bobbi Wilson and her parents (Both photos by Andrew Hurley, Yale University). ALTHOUGH BORN FOUR CENTURIES APART, CONSIDERATION OF MERIAN AND WILSON HIGHLIGHTS THE RACIAL AND GENDER INEQUALITIES THAT STILL PLAGUE SCIENCE TODAY. Reflecting on Merian’s life and her passion for arthropods shines a light on the story of Bobbi Wilson, a young Black girl with a fascination for spotted lanternflies, who was wrongfully reported to local police by a neighbor while harvesting specimens from the sidewalk of her neighborhood (Poitras 2023). This report was an overt act of racism. Bobbi, a 9-year-old girl, was reported as an adult Black woman by a White neighbor, Gordon Lawshe. It was stated that “Lawshe saw something scary. Recognizing it was not an emergency per se, he called the police department dispatcher instead. ‘There’s a little Black woman walking, spraying stuff on the sidewalks and trees on Elizabeth and Florence,’ Lawshe told the dispatcher. ‘I don’t know what the hell she’s doing. Scares me, though,’ Lawshe added” (Romo 2023). The adultification of young Black children has been a dangerously common practice across the United States and still persists today. Racial profiling puts children at risk for trauma and police violence. While the police officers involved handled the situation calmly, the experience is extremely impactful at a personal and societal level, as it shows the obstacles a Black girl encounters while following her passion for science. Although born four centuries apart, consideration of Merian and Wilson highlights the racial and gender inequalities that still plague science today. Both Merian and Wilson remind us that scientific discovery is attainable and literally right at one’s doorstep if one has an inquisitive mind and determined spirit, but hurdles persist. Challenging 17th-century scientific tenets or being a young Black girl showing interest in science in the 21st century can be seen as threatening by some members of society. Today, individuals at scientific institutions must all actively strive to break down structural inequities in scientific education and make scientific discovery a more accessible and inclusive space. The author would like to thank Lawrence Gall, Ph.D., for discussions, Jennifer Barrer-Gall and Kelly Morrow for reading the manuscript and helpful suggestions, and Stephen Lory, Ph.D., for encouraging journal submission.

title: Aboriginal Peoples and Terrestrial Invertebrates in Australia: Historical and Cultural RelationshipsBy Philip A.Clarke, CSIRO Publishing, Melbourne. ISBN 9781486320431 334 pages, with 60 colour pictures
abstract: Aboriginal peoples have deep connections with Australia's terrestrial invertebrates. The different tribes value insects and other terrestrial arthropods as food, as totemic ancestors, creators and spirit beings, and as sources for materials and medicines. In this book anthropologist and ethnobiologist Philip Clarke, focuses on these nutritional, cultural and practical relationships. Using a historian's approach, Clarke has consulted a very wide range of sources, including documents from early explorers, conversations with Aboriginal elders and scientific publications. Among these sources, the studies of two researchers feature prominently. Firstly, the publications of the very productive Norman Tindale (1900–1993) are heavily cited. Tindale was an anthropologist, but also a hepialid (Lepidoptera) taxonomist, a group that contains some of the species with ‘witchetty grub’ larvae (however, most witchetty grubs are cossid moths, and some are even cerambycid larvae—see below). Secondly, the work of Alan Yen (1950–2017) receives much attention. Alan was an entomologist, conservationist, and invertebrate ecologist and an active member of the Australian Entomological Society. The Society's conservation award is named in his honour. In addition to his focus on conservation Alan published papers on insects as human food. Clarke's book brings together an immense number of terrestrial invertebrate species, and explores how they have been named, classified, foraged for, used, and celebrated by the many different Aboriginal cultures. For those interested in ethno-entomology, this overview of terrestrial invertebrates as sources of food, medicine, storytelling and spiritual significance for Aboriginal Peoples is a goldmine of information. In the introductory chapter, the stark differences in the traditional Aboriginal knowledge of invertebrates as food and the European classification of a largely unknown invertebrate fauna is noted, together with cultural differences and disinclination of early explorers to record them as food (as opposed to hunting vertebrates). Where possible, Clarke has included the current scientific names for the invertebrates mentioned. Not surprisingly, there were many profound difficulties in identifying the species or even their families. One of these problems was that at the time of the early explorers almost no Australian species had been described. This led to vague documentation and a tendency to refer Australian invertebrates using European classifications. For example, the early reports often referred to mygalomorph spiders as ‘Tarantulas’ but the same term could also indicate Wolf- or Huntsman spiders (collectively representing three different spider families). In addition, the spoken dialects were often incorrectly put into writing or wrongly translated into English. Furthermore, the classification itself could be sacred and hence not revealed, and local names could disappear, for example after a person with the same or a similar sounding name had died. Sadly, in many cases this cannot be traced back, because languages, as well as cultural knowledge have also disappeared. Clarke notes that ongoing collaboration between indigenous speakers, linguists and scientists is contributing to dictionaries, that together with reinforcement through lived experience, aims to increase the transmission of cultural knowledge. This compendium of information is written factually and concisely, as text in sentence form. It occurred to us that much of the data could have been presented as a series of Tables, which may have made searching for specific information easier, but obviously would have been less entertaining to read! In Chapter 2, it becomes clear that the various Indigenous classifications often neither matched each other nor the scientific ones. For example, some tribes classified food sources after the type of food: vertebrate, invertebrates and plants. Others classified them according to a range of different criteria such as behaviour, their place in the environment or their associations to plants. For example, criteria for classifications included: movement (leading to groupings of flying birds, bats and insects, slithering snakes and worms, and crawling beetles and spiders); the production of sound (Orthoptera, Cicadidae and tree frogs); the production of silk (various caterpillars and spiders); or production of sugar (sugarbag bees and honey ants). Then there were classifications based on place or ecological niche (e.g., whirligig beetles and turtles) or their plant host (e.g., witchetty grubs). The author warns against comparing the Indigenous and Western scientific perspective on classification and the environment in general, as one is dominated by ancestral traditions and life experiences, while the other is based on established scientific principles. Chapter 3, titled ‘Terrestrial invertebrates as creators and spirit beings’ provides a selection of the wealth of Aboriginal Mythology on insects and allied arthropods. The chapter includes stories about invertebrates as creation ancestors and spirit beings. Many of these are invertebrate species that were either encountered often in daily life, or major sources of food, medicine and useful materials. The chapter contains stories about grubs and galls, caterpillars and butterflies, sugarbag bees, ants, termites, spiders and nuisance invertebrates such as lice, botflies, ticks, mosquitoes, leeches (including a ‘leech dreaming’!). We were surprised that the totemic systems of Aboriginal Australia were teeming with terrestrial invertebrates. This clearly reflects their fundamental importance for sustenance and survival and highlights their cultural significance. The ensuing four chapters comprise regional information on foraging for certain groups of invertebrates. The chapters cover woodboring grubs (Chapter 4), moths (including the iconic ghost moths and bogong moths of southern temperate and alpine Australia, respectively), butterflies and galls (Chapter 5), bees (including anecdotal observations by Aboriginal peoples that the European honeybee had detrimentally affected native bees) and ants (Chapter 6), and termites, lerps and other terrestrial invertebrates (Chapter 7). As noted, the nomenclature used by Aboriginal people may often differ between adults and larvae of the same species (creating two ethnospecies from one biological species) or aggregating similar life forms, e.g., ‘grubs’ (forming one ethnospecies from multiple biological species). As well as recording the identity of species, each of these chapters detail their importance as a food source, laws and strategies around foraging and food preparation, as well as the environmental impact of foraging practises. In Chapter 8 ‘Terrestrial invertebrates working for people’, details how terrestrial invertebrates were used for purposes other than a source of food. This included using distribution of ant nests to assess the likelihood of flooding, or forecasting seasonal change, studying the behaviour of wasps, bees and ants to find water, nectar or vertebrate prey. Furthermore, worms and insects, in particular larvae, were used as baits or lures for catching fish or even birds. Seeds were collected from ant granaries, which saved labour. Woodboring grubs, caterpillars, galls cockroaches and beetles were used to provide various skin and wound treatments. Termites and termite soil were used in a wide range of ways, maggots were used for cleaning wounds, and honey, pollen, eggs, wax and waste from sugarbag bees provided cures for general sickness, eye sores, festering wounds, and tinea. Chapter 9, ‘Material culture’ features (among other applications) using ants to make glue, the many uses of bees wax, the use of wasps, ants and termite nests as sources of clay for hearths and earth ovens, and molluscs for tools and spider web for cord. In addition, the chapter includes cultural applications such as molluscs as ornaments, spider web as ritual tools, and dry hard galls as marbles. The chapter also briefly mentions the sacred imagery of invertebrate ancestors, as well as the importance of termites for making digeridoos. The final chapter details the differences in attitude of Europeans and Aboriginal peoples regarding the consumption of terrestrial invertebrates, and explains that the development of a deeper understanding of Aboriginal relationships with terrestrial invertebrates serves an important contemporary need. It emphasises the symbolic importance of invertebrates such as the Yeperenye totem of central Australia, the frequent depiction of invertebrates such as witchetty grubs and honey ants in art and the enormous reliance on invertebrates as food. The chapter observes the growing popularity of ‘bush tucker’ as a niche market in ecotourism and the specialist restaurant industry, with a corresponding cautionary note on invertebrate conservation and the sustainability of ‘wild harvest’. The chapter concludes with the prophetic observation that invertebrates are integral to building and maintaining Indigenous cultural identities. In summary, for persons with an interest in ethno-entomology this book is an absolute treasure trove of information, gleaned from a career-long accumulation of literature and observations. Each of these observations are meticulously cited at the end of each chapter, and referenced in full, with an impressive 978 references concluding the book! The book is illustrated with 60 colour images (as 30 colour plates) and well-illustrated with line drawings throughout the text. However, we do not only admire the book for its content—we are in awe of the way Clarke has managed to structure this plethora of very diverse facts. This is an admirable feat as, there are many tribes with different cultures and languages, very many terrestrial invertebrates, all with different distributions, requiring different foraging techniques and having different uses. Additionally, many of the explorers and early ethnobiologists did not have names for the invertebrates they found, and Philip Clarke has tried to attach current scientific names to all species. Importantly, this book explores, rather than ignores, the gaps between the knowledge systems of Indigenous peoples and Western science. It does so very respectfully, with the aim to encourage acknowledgement, understanding, and future collaboration. Philip Clarke wrote a very informative, readable and well-documented book about terrestrial invertebrates and their significance for Aboriginal people. Clarke, Philip A., 2026. ‘Aboriginal Peoples and Terrestrial Invertebrates in Australia: Historical and Cultural Relationships’, CSIRO Publishing, Melbourne. ISBN 9781486320431 334 pages, with 60 colour pictures.
